<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
We define the delta set as \[\Delta (S_h) = \{ l_2 -l_1 : l_2,l_1 \in L(s), L(s) \cap (l_1,l_2) = \emptyset \} \]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
We define the subtractive Euclidean Algorithm in this way: Let \[x_0 \ and \ y_0 \ = (e,d)\]
Recursively define 
\[
(x_{i+1},y_{i+1})=
\begin{cases}
(x_i-y_i,y_i),& x_i>y_i,\\
(x_i,y_i-x_i),& y_i>x_i,\\
\text{terminate},& x_i=y_i.
\end{cases} \]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The case $k=2$ gives
\[
S_h=\langle a,ah+d,ah+2d\rangle .
\]
 In this case, Theorem~\ref{thm:maintheorem} gives the same description of the delta set obtained by Garc\'ia-S\'anchez,
Llena, and Moscariello for symmetric and nonsymmetric numerical semigroups
of embedding dimension three
\cite{GarciaLlenaMoscarielloSym,GarciaLlenaMoscarielloNonSym}. Set\ \(
e=h-1
\ \text{and} \ 
M=\left\lceil\frac{a}{2}\right\rceil e+d.
\)
Then Theorem~\ref{thm:maintheorem} gives
\[
\Delta(S_h)
=
E(e,d)\cup
\{M-re:M-re>0,\ r\geq0\}, \  \textnormal{or equivalently,} \ E(M,e)
\]

Comparing this with the results of
\cite{GarciaLlenaMoscarielloSym,GarciaLlenaMoscarielloNonSym}, we consider the
relation lattice of $S_h$. Using their framework,
\[
c_1=d+h\left\lceil\frac{a}{2}\right\rceil,
\qquad
c_2=2,
\qquad
c_3=\left\lceil\frac{a}{2}\right\rceil,
\]
with
\[
r_{12}=r_{32}=a\bmod 2,\qquad
r_{13}=\left\lfloor\frac{a}{2}\right\rfloor,
\]
\[
r_{21}=h,\qquad
r_{23}=1,\qquad
r_{31}=h\left\lfloor\frac{a}{2}\right\rfloor+d.
\]
In particular,
\[
c_1n_1=c_3n_3
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\equiv0\pmod 2.
\]
$S_h$ is then symmetric if and only if $a$ is even. Hence, both the
symmetric and nonsymmetric cases are described by the two results of
Garc\'ia-S\'anchez, Llena, and Moscariello
\cite{GarciaLlenaMoscarielloSym,GarciaLlenaMoscarielloNonSym}.

Their Euclidean-algorithm invariants collapse into
\[
(\delta_1,\delta_2)=(M,e)
\qquad\text{if $a$ is even},
\]
while
\[
(\delta_1,\delta_3)=(M,M-e)
\qquad\text{if $a$ is odd}.
\]
Although the two pairs appear different, they produce the same delta set, since

\[
M\geq 2e+d>2e,
\]
so the first subtractive Euclidean step applied to $(M,M-e)$ gives
\[
(M,M-e)\longmapsto(M-e,e).
\]
Thus the subsequent Euclidean algorithm is the same as that obtained from
$(M,e)$.

It remains to compare this Euclidean description with the decomposition
in Theorem~\ref{thm:maintheorem}. Since
\[
M=\left\lceil\frac{a}{2}\right\rceil e+d
\equiv d\pmod e,
\]
the subtractive Euclidean algorithm applied to $(M,e)$ first produces the
values
\[
\{M-re:M-re>0,\ r\geq0\},
\]
until the remainder modulo $e$ is reached. The remaining Euclidean steps
are precisely those obtained from $(e,d\bmod e)$. Therefore
\[
\Delta(S_h)
=
\{M-re:M-re>0,\ r\geq0\}
\cup E(e,d\bmod e).
\]
Since the subtractive Euclidean algorithm is unchanged by replacing $d$
with its residue modulo $e$, 
\[
E(e,d\bmod e)=E(e,d).
\]
Hence the Euclidean-algorithm description in
\cite{GarciaLlenaMoscarielloSym,GarciaLlenaMoscarielloNonSym}
agrees exactly with Theorem~\ref{thm:maintheorem}.

For example, let
\[
a=4,\qquad h=143,\qquad d=109.
\]
Then
\[
S_h=\langle4,681,790\rangle,
\qquad e=142,
\qquad M=393.
\]
The arithmetic-progression component is
\[
\{M-142r:M-142r>0\}
=
\{393,251,109\},
\]
while the remaining values are obtained from the subtractive Euclidean
algorithm applied to $(109,142)$. This gives
\[
\Delta(S_h)
=
\{1,2,3,4,7,10,13,23,33,43,76,109,142,251,393\},
\]
in agreement with \cite[Example 38]{GarciaLlenaMoscarielloSym}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
There exists
\[\mu_s\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,a-1\}\]
such that $Z(s)$ is in bijection with
\[R_s=\left\{(j,y)\in\mathbb{N}^2:L_j\leq y\leq U_j\right\},\]
where
\[L_j= \left\lceil \frac{\mu_s+aj}{k} \right\rceil, \]
and \(U_j= \min\left\{\mu_s+aj,\left\lfloor\frac{s-d(\mu_s+aj)}{ah} \right\rfloor\right\}.\)

We define the factorization length
$l_s(j,l)=C_s-d\mu_s-ey,$ where \(C_s=\frac{s-d\mu_s}{a}.\)
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since
\[s=ax+\sum_{i=1}^{k} (ah+id)y_i,\]
this can be simplified as
\[s=ax+ah\sum_{i=1}^{k}y_i +d\sum_{i=1}^{k}iy_i =ax+ahy+dm.\]

This equation implies \(s\equiv dm\pmod a.\) Furthermore, since
\(\gcd(a,d)=1,\)
there exists some
\(\mu_s\in\{0,1,\ldots,a-1\}\)
such that
\(s\equiv d\mu_s\pmod a.\) Therefore,
\(m\equiv\mu_s\pmod a.\) So, \(m=aj+\mu_s, j\geq0.\)
Connecting m to \(y\)
via
\(
y\leq m\leq ky,
\)
we have
\(\left\lceil\frac{m}{k}\right\rceil \leq y\leq m.\) Additionally, since
\(
x\geq0,
\)
\(s\geq ahy+dm\implies \frac{s-dm}{ah}\geq y,\) creating yet another upper bound on $y.$ 
Since \[m=\mu_s+aj,\] the lower bound of $y$ then becomes
\[
\left\lceil \frac{\mu_s+aj}{k} \right\rceil,
\]
while the upper bound becomes
\[
\min\left\{
\mu_s+aj,\,
\left\lfloor
\frac{s-d(\mu_s+aj)}{ah}
\right\rfloor
\right\}.
\]
This proves both the upper and lower bounds of $y$. Solving for x in $s=ax+ahy+dm$ and substituting that in, 
\[l_s=x+y= \frac{s-dm-ahy}{ah}+y = \frac{s-d(\mu_s+aj)-ahy}{ah}+y.\]
Substituting $C_s,$
\[l_s= C_s-dj-ey.\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:column-threshold}
There exists some
\(
j^{\dagger}
\)
such that
\(j\leq j^{\dagger} \text{are unconstrained} \)
and
\(j\geq j^{\dagger}\text{is constrained}.\)
\begin{proof}
The budgeted upper bound
\(B_j= \left\lfloor \frac{s-d(\mu_s+aj)}{ah} \right\rfloor\)
has slope \(-\frac{d}{ah},\)
while the unconstrained bound
\(\mu_s+aj\)
has slope $a$. $a>- \frac{d}{ah}.$ Therefore, once
\(B_j<\mu_s+aj,\)
this inequality will continue to hold for all larger $j$.
\end{proof}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The budgeted upper bound
\(B_j= \left\lfloor \frac{s-d(\mu_s+aj)}{ah} \right\rfloor\)
has slope \(-\frac{d}{ah},\)
while the unconstrained bound
\(\mu_s+aj\)
has slope $a$. $a>- \frac{d}{ah}.$ Therefore, once
\(B_j<\mu_s+aj,\)
this inequality will continue to hold for all larger $j$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\[\operatorname{Max}(j) \equiv C_s-dj \pmod e. \]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This is immediate from the formula
\[ \operatorname{Max}(j) = C_s-dj-eL_j. \]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
For a numerical monoid $S$,
\[
\max(\Delta(S))
=
\max_{n\in\operatorname{Betti}(S)}
\left(\max(\Delta(n))\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
Set
\[
r \equiv a-1 \pmod{k}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
p=\frac{a-1-r}{k}.
\]
Then the Betti elements occur in the form
\[
pn_k+n_j,
\qquad r+1\leq j\leq k.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We begin with the initial equality:$$a(qh+d) = ax + ahY + dW$$Taking both sides modulo $a$:$$dW \equiv 0 \pmod a$$Given that $\gcd(a, d) = 1$, $a$ must divide $W$. Thus, there exists an integer $m$ such that:$$W = ma$$Substituting $W = ma$ back into the main equation:$$a(qh+d) = ax + ahY + d(ma)$$Dividing both sides by $a$:$$qh + d = x + hY + dm$$ To isolate the quantity $x + Y,$ which represents total length, we rewrite $hY$ as $(h- 1)Y + Y$:$$qh + d = x + Y + h(Y - 1) + dm$$ $$x + Y = qh + d - dm - Y(h - 1)$$3. If $m = 0$, then $W = ma = 0$, which implies $Y = 0$. Substituting $m = 0$ and $Y = 0$ into the expression gives:$$x + Y = x=  qh + d$$Because the length is minimized with $-dm = 0,$ $qh + d$ represents the maximum possible value. For $m \ge 1$, we use the relation $W \le kY$ (relation comes since $i \neq k$ always):$$ma \le kY \implies Y \ge \frac{am}{k}$$Given $q = \left\lceil \frac{a}{k} \right\rceil$, it follows that $Y \ge q$ for $m \ge 1.$ Substituting the lower bound $Y \ge q$ back into our isolated expression for $x + Y$:$$x + Y = qh + d(1 - m) - Y(h - 1) \ge qh + d(1 - m) - q(h - 1)$$Simplifying the right-hand side:$$qh + d(1 - m) - qh + q = d(1 - m) + q$$Thus, for $m \ge 1$:$$x + Y \ge d(1 - m) + q$$ Because no integer values of $m$ exist strictly between the bound for $m = 1$ ($q$) and the bound for $m = 0$ ($qh + d$), these lengths are therefore consecutive.
It now remains to show that no other Betti element produces a larger
delta.  For
\[
n_k=ah+kd
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n_j=ah+jd,
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_j
&=p(ah+kd)+(ah+jd)\\
&=(p+1)ah+(pk+j)d.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $j=r+i$ and $pk+r=a-1$,
\[
pk+j=pk+r+i=a-1+i.
\]
Therefore,
\[
b_j=qha+(a-1+i)d.
\]
Rewriting this expression gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_j
&=(qh+d-h)a+\bigl(ha+(i-1)d\bigr)\\
&=(qh+d-h)a+n_{i-1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where $n_0=a$.

Thus $b_j$ has a factorization of length
\[
qh+d-h+1.
\]
Comparing this with the factorization of length $q$ gives
\[
qh+d-h+1-q
=
(q-1)(h-1)+d.
\]
Since $h>1$,
\[
(q-1)(h-1)+d
\leq
q(h-1)+d.
\]
Hence these Betti elements cannot produce a delta larger than
\[
q(h-1)+d.
\]

The remaining Betti elements described by Omidali and Rahmati
arise from relations of the form
\[
n_i+n_j=n_u+n_v.
\]
If $s \in S= n_i+n_j,$ it can also be written as $s = hn_0+n_{i+j},$ where $h$ is the number of copies of $a.$
Thus, $s$ either has length difference $h-1 \ or \ 2-2=0$. In either case, the length is strictly less than  $q(h-1)+d$. 

We have therefore shown that
\[
\max_{n\in\operatorname{Betti}(S)}\max(\Delta(n))
=
q(h-1)+d.
\]
Applying the first lemma and recalling that
$q=\left\lceil a/k\right\rceil$, we obtain the following theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Maximal Delta]
For
\[
S_h=\langle a,ah+d,ah+2d,\ldots,ah+kd\rangle,
\]
where $\gcd(a,d)=1$, $1<k<a$, and $h >1$,
\[
\boxed{
\max(\Delta(S_h))
=
\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil(h-1)+d
}.
\]
\end{theorem}



\begin{corollary}
\medskip
Omidali \cite{Omidali} proved that the catenary degree is of the form

 \[ \left\lceil \frac{a}{k} \right\rceil (h)+d\]

 Combining that with our theorem, we get that
 
 \[ max(\Delta(S)) + \left\lceil \frac{a}{k} \right\rceil = c(S),\] 
 
 
\end{corollary}
which additionally provides a new result in regards to calculating the catenary degree.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
For
\[
S_h=\langle a,ah+d,ah+2d,\ldots,ah+kd\rangle,
\]
where $\gcd(a,d)=1$, $1<k<a$, and $h >1$,
\[
\boxed{
\max(\Delta(S_h))
=
\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil(h-1)+d
}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\medskip
Omidali \cite{Omidali} proved that the catenary degree is of the form

 \[ \left\lceil \frac{a}{k} \right\rceil (h)+d\]

 Combining that with our theorem, we get that
 
 \[ max(\Delta(S)) + \left\lceil \frac{a}{k} \right\rceil = c(S),\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:boundary-difference-index-mapping}

Suppose that the columns $C_j$ and $C_{j+1}$ (defined in Section 6) are both unconstrained and that
\[\operatorname{Min}(j)>\operatorname{Max}(j+1).\]
Let
\[m_j=\mu_s+aj, \qquad q=\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil. \]
Define
\[\widetilde r(m) = q-\left\lceil\frac{m+a}{k}\right\rceil+m, \qquad m\geq 0.\]
Then
\[\operatorname{Min}(j)-\operatorname{Max}(j+1)=M-e\widetilde r(m_j).\]
Moreover, the sequence $\{\widetilde r(m)\}_{m\geq 0}$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\widetilde r(0)=0$;
    \item $\widetilde r(m+1)-\widetilde r(m)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $m\geq0$;
    \item $\widetilde r(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently,
\(
\{\widetilde r(m):m\geq0\}=\mathbb N_0.
\)
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Since $C_j$ and $C_{j+1}$ are unconstrained, their upper and lower
endpoints are given by
\(
U_j=m_j \ \text{and} \ 
L_{j+1}
=
\left\lceil\frac{m_j+a}{k}\right\rceil.
\)
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Min}(j)-\operatorname{Max}(j+1)
&=
\bigl(C_s-dj-eU_j\bigr)
-
\bigl(C_s-d(j+1)-eL_{j+1}\bigr)\\
&=
d+e(L_{j+1}-U_j).
\end{align*}
Since
\(
M=qe+d,
\)
this introduces a similarity with the form $M-re.$
Set
\(
M-re=d+e(L_{j+1}-U_j).
\)
Equating the two expressions and cancelling $d$ gives
\(qe-re=e(L_{j+1}-U_j),
\)
and hence
\[
r=q-L_{j+1}+U_j.
\]
Substituting the expressions for $L_{j+1}$ and $U_j$ yields
\(r = q-\left\lceil\frac{m_j+a}{k}\right\rceil+m_j = \widetilde r(m_j). \)
Thus
\[\operatorname{Min}(j)-\operatorname{Max}(j+1) = M-e\widetilde r(m_j). \]

It remains to establish the stated properties of $\widetilde r$.

First, \(\widetilde r(0) = q-\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil = 0,\)
by the definition of $q$.

Next, for every $m\geq0$,
\begin{align*}
\widetilde r(m+1)-\widetilde r(m)
&=
\left[
q-\left\lceil\frac{m+1+a}{k}\right\rceil+(m+1)
\right]
-
\left[
q-\left\lceil\frac{m+a}{k}\right\rceil+m
\right]\\
&=
1-
\left(
\left\lceil\frac{m+a+1}{k}\right\rceil
-
\left\lceil\frac{m+a}{k}\right\rceil
\right).
\end{align*}
Since increasing the numerator of a ceiling by $1$ can increase the
ceiling by either $0$ or $1$, we have
\[\left\lceil\frac{m+a+1}{k}\right\rceil - \left\lceil\frac{m+a}{k}\right\rceil \in\{0,1\}.\]
Consequently,
\(\widetilde r(m+1)-\widetilde r(m)\in\{0,1\}. \)

Finally, using
\[ \left\lceil x\right\rceil<x+1, \]
we obtain
\begin{align*}
\widetilde r(m)
&=
q-\left\lceil\frac{m+a}{k}\right\rceil+m\\
&>
q-\left(\frac{m+a}{k}+1\right)+m\\
&=
m\left(1-\frac1k\right)
+
\left(q-\frac ak-1\right).
\end{align*}
Since $k\geq2$, we have $1-\frac1k>0$, and therefore
\[\widetilde r(m)\longrightarrow\infty \qquad\text{as }m\to\infty. \]

Thus $\widetilde r(m)$ is a nondecreasing, unbounded sequence of
nonnegative integers, beginning at $0$, whose successive increments
are at most $1$. It follows that the sequence cannot skip any
nonnegative integer. This becomes important when studying the entire subset generated by \[M-re\]
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:consecutive-boundary-extrema}
Suppose that the columns $C_j$ and $C_{j+1}$ are both unconstrained and
that
\[\operatorname{Min}(j)>\operatorname{Max}(j+1).\]
Then $\operatorname{Max}(j+1)$ and $\operatorname{Min}(j)$ are
consecutive elements of $L(s)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Every element of $C_j$
is at least $\operatorname{Min}(j)$, while every element of
$C_{j+1}$ is at most $\operatorname{Max}(j+1)$. Thus neither $C_j$ nor
$C_{j+1}$ contains an element strictly between
$\operatorname{Max}(j+1)$ and $\operatorname{Min}(j)$.

Now consider a column $C_r$ with $r<j$. By the budget column lemma (6.1.),
every column between $C_r$ and $C_{j+1}$ is unconstrained. In
particular, the column $C_r$ lies strictly to the left of $C_j$, and
the ordering of \(U_j\) gives
\[\operatorname{Min}(r)>\operatorname{Min}(j).\]
Hence every element of $C_r$ is strictly greater than
$\operatorname{Min}(j)$.

On the other hand, if $r>j+1$, the decrease of \(L_j\) implies
\[\operatorname{Max}(r)<\operatorname{Max}(j+1).\]
Therefore every element of $C_r$ is strictly smaller than
$\operatorname{Max}(j+1)$.

Combining these observations, no element of $L(s)$ lies strictly
between $\operatorname{Max}(j+1)$ and $\operatorname{Min}(j)$. Since
both endpoints belong to $L(s)$, they are consecutive elements of
$L(s)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:boundary-family}
We have
\[\left\{M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0\right\}\subseteq \Delta(S_h).\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Fix $r\geq0$ such that
\[M-re>0.\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-difference-index-mapping}, the map
$\widetilde r:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb N_0$ is surjective. Hence there
exists $m\geq0$ such that
\[\widetilde r(m)=r.\]
If we then choose a corresponding $\mu_s$ in the residue class, and then choose an element $s$ large enough so that both
 \(C_j, \ C_{j+1}\)are both unconstrained, Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-difference-index-mapping}
gives
\(\operatorname{Min}(j)-\operatorname{Max}(j+1)=M-e\widetilde r(m)=M-er.\)
 $M-er>0$, and hence
\(\operatorname{Min}(j)>\operatorname{Max}(j+1).\)
Lemma~\ref{lem:consecutive-boundary-extrema} therefore implies that
$\operatorname{Max}(j+1)$ and $\operatorname{Min}(j)$ are consecutive
elements of $L(s)$. Their difference is consequently an element of
$\Delta(S_h)$, so
\[M-er\in\Delta(S_h).\]

Since $r\geq0$ with $M-er>0$ was arbitrary, we conclude that
\[\left\{M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0 \right\} \subseteq \Delta(S_h).\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\textnormal{Suppose first that}
\[e\mid d.\]
\textnormal{We write}
\[d=ce.\]
Then
\[E(e,d) =\{e,2e,\ldots,ce\}.\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Set
\[r=q+c-i.\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
M-re
&=
M-(q+c-i)e \\
&=
qe+ce-(q+c-i)e \\
&=
ie.
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:euclidean-gap}
By the Three-Gap Theorem and the subtractive Euclidean algorithm,
\[
\bigcup_{J\geq 1}G_J=E(e,\rho).
\]
Alternatively, every gap $g\in G_J $ created by inserting a new point $j$ and then finding $j\rho \pmod e$ splits the current gap between $j's$ so that it conforms to the subtractive Euclidean Algorithm.
Since \(E(e,d)=E(e,\rho)\), it is therefore enough to prove that every
\[
g\in G_J
\]
belongs to \(\Delta(S_h)\).
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\[
\forall s\in S, s=aC_s+d\mu_s.
\]
Setting
\(\mu_s=0,\),
\(
s=aC_s.
\)

\[\ell(j,y)\equiv C-dj\pmod e.\]
Since
\[d\equiv \rho\pmod e,\]
we have
\[C-dj\equiv C-j\rho\pmod e.\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\textnormal{Now choose \(j_0\), and consider the consecutive columns}
\[j_0,j_0+1,\ldots,j_0+J-1.\]
\textnormal{After translating all residues by the fixed quantity \(C-dj_0\), the residue classes in these columns are exactly the elements of \(P_J\). Therefore, since \(g\in G_J\), there exist}
\[r_1,r_2\in\{0,\ldots,J-1\}\]
\textnormal{such that, with
\[j_1=j_0+r_1,\qquad j_2=j_0+r_2,\]
the residue classes corresponding to \(j_1\) and \(j_2\) are consecutive and have cyclic separation \(g\). Our goal is to "lift" this modular difference into a difference of actual lengths.}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
Let \(R_i\in\{0,\ldots,e-1\}\) denote the residue of \(C-dj_i\) modulo \(e\). Thus
\[C-dj_i=R_i+eQ_i\]
for some \(Q_i\in\mathbb Z\). \textnormal{Since the two residue classes have cyclic separation \(g\), we may write
\[R_2-R_1=g+te\]
for some} \(t\in\mathbb Z\).

For a lattice point \((j_i,y_i)\), we have
\[\ell_i = C-dj_i-ey_i = R_i-e(y_i-Q_i). \]
Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_i'&=y_i-Q_i,\\
\ell_i&=R_i-ey_i',\\
\ell_2-\ell_1
&=(R_2-R_1)-e(y_2'-y_1').
\end{aligned}
\]
Using
\(R_2-R_1=g+te,
\)
we see that
\[
\ell_2-\ell_1=g
\quad\text{when}\quad
y_2'-y_1'=t.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
y_2-y_1=t+Q_2-Q_1.
\]
Set
\[
\alpha=t+Q_2-Q_1.
\]

Since
\[
Q_i=\frac{C-dj_i-R_i}{e},
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_2-Q_1
&=\frac{-d(j_2-j_1)-(R_2-R_1)}{e}\\
&=\frac{-d(r_2-r_1)-g-te}{e}\\
&=-q(r_2-r_1)
-\frac{\rho(r_2-r_1)+g}{e}-t,
\end{aligned}
\]
where we have used
\[
j_2-j_1=r_2-r_1,
\qquad
R_2-R_1=g+te,
\qquad
d=qe+\rho.
\]
The residue relation between the two consecutive points gives
\[
w=\frac{\rho(r_2-r_1)+g}{e}\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Therefore
\[
Q_2-Q_1=-q(r_2-r_1)-w-t,
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\alpha=-q(r_2-r_1)-w.}
\]

In particular, the \(t\)-terms cancel. Moreover,
\[
|r_2-r_1|\leq J-1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|w|\leq J-1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{|\alpha|\leq(q+1)(J-1).}
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
We now choose \(C\) sufficiently large so that
\[
C\geq(ah+d)(j_0+J-1).
\]
This would then allow
\[
U_j=aj
,\]
which would further generate the allowable \(y\)-coordinates in column \(j\) to be precisely
\[
I_j=\left[\left\lceil\frac{aj}{k}\right\rceil,aj\right]\cap\mathbb Z.
\]

If we then choose \(j_0\) sufficiently large, there exist allowable lattice points
\[
(j_1,y_1),
\qquad
(j_2,y_2)
\]
satisfying
\[
y_2-y_1=\alpha.
\]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
By the definition of \(\alpha\),
\[
y_2'-y_1'=t.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_2-\ell_1
&=(R_2-R_1)-e(y_2'-y_1')\\
&=(g+te)-et\\
&=g.
\end{aligned}
\] \textbf{Thus} \(g\) \textbf{is a difference of factorization lengths.}

\textnormal{Finally, because the residue classes corresponding to \(j_1\) and \(j_2\) are consecutive elements of \(P_J\), there is no residue class between them. Hence there is no factorization length strictly between the two constructed lengths. Therefore, they are consecutive elements of the length set \(L(s)\), and so}
\[g=\ell_2-\ell_1\in\Delta(S_h).\]

Since \(g\in G_J\) was arbitrary, we conclude that
\[G_J\subseteq\Delta(S_h)\]
for every \(J\geq1\).
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{corollary:Euclidean-Inclusion}
\[
E(e,\rho)=\bigcup_{J\geq1}G_J\subseteq\Delta(S_h).
\]
Finally, since
\[E(e,d)=E(e,\rho),\]
we obtain
\[
\boxed{E(e,d)\subseteq\Delta(S_h).}
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:trunc}
Let $x<y$ be consecutive elements of $\mathcal L(s)$ with
\[
x\in C_i,\qquad y\in C_j.
\]
If
\[
y-x>e,
\]
then
\[
x=\operatorname{Max}(i),\qquad
y=\operatorname{Min}(j),\qquad
j<i.
\]
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose first that
\(
x<\operatorname{Max}(i).
\)
Since $C_i$ is an arithmetic progression of common difference $e$,
the element $x+e$ also belongs to $C_i$. Since $y-x>e$, we have
\(x<x+e<y,\)
contradicting the assumption that $x$ and $y$ are consecutive.
Therefore
\(
x=\operatorname{Max}(i).
\) Similarly, if
\(
y>\operatorname{Min}(j),
\)
then $y-e\in C_j$ and
\(
x<y-e<y,
\)
again contradicting consecutiveness. Hence
\(y=\operatorname{Min}(j).\)


\(\operatorname{Max}(i)=x<y=\operatorname{Min}(j)
\leq \operatorname{Max}(j).\)
But this is impossible when $i<j$. Consequently,
\(
j<i.
\)
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:gapbound}
Let $x<y$ be consecutive elements of $\mathcal L(s)$ with
\[
x\in C_i,\qquad y\in C_j,\qquad i<j.
\]
Then
\[
0<y-x\leq e.
\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Clearly $y-x>0$. If $y-x>e$, Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc} would imply
$j<i$, contradicting $i<j$. Hence
\(
0<y-x\leq e.
\)
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:survival}
Let $x<y$ be consecutive elements of $\mathcal L(s)$ with
\[
x\in C_i,\qquad y\in C_j,\qquad J=j-i\geq1.
\]
Then, for every $1\leq t\leq J$,
\[
L_{i+t}\leq \ell_i-m_t\leq U_{i+t}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x+o_t
=
C_s-d(i+t)-e(\ell_i-m_t)
\in C_{i+t}\subseteq\mathcal L(s).
\]
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The identity follows directly from \[
\begin{aligned}
C_s-d(i+t)-e(\ell_i-m_t)
&=
C_s-di-e\ell_i-dt+em_t\\
&=
x+o_t.
\end{aligned}
\]
The inequality $L_{i+t} \leq \ell_i-m_t \leq U_{i+t}$ ensures that $ x+ o_t$ is an allowable value, and it therefore remains necessary to prove that $ \ell_i -m_t$ is within the allowable length values.

We first prove the upper bound.

Since
\(
\ell_i\leq U_i\leq\mu+ai,
\)
we have
\(
\ell_i-m_t<\mu+a(i+t),
\)
and hence
\[
\ell_i-m_t\leq\mu+a(i+t). \tag{10.3}
\]

Also,
\(
\ell_i\leq U_i\leq B_i.
\)
Furthermore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_i-B_{i+t}
&=
\left\lfloor\frac{C_s-di}{h}\right\rfloor
-
\left\lfloor\frac{C_s-di-dt}{h}\right\rfloor\\
&\leq
\left\lfloor\frac{dt}{h}\right\rfloor+1\\
&\leq
\left\lceil\frac{dt}{e}\right\rceil\\
&=
m_t.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
B_i-m_t\leq B_{i+t},
\]
and hence
\[
\ell_i-m_t
\leq B_i-m_t
\leq B_{i+t}. \tag{9.4}
\]
Combining (9.3) and (9.4) yields
\[
\ell_i-m_t\leq U_{i+t}.
\]

We now prove the lower bound.

Since $x<y$,
\(
-dJ+e(\ell_i-\ell_j)>0.
\)
Thus
\(
e(\ell_i-\ell_j)>dJ,
\)
so
\(
\ell_i-\ell_j
\geq
\left\lceil\frac{dJ+1}{e}\right\rceil.
\)
Because
\(
\left\lceil\frac{dJ+1}{e}\right\rceil
\geq
\left\lceil\frac{dJ}{e}\right\rceil
=m_J,
\)
we obtain
\(
\ell_i-m_J\geq\ell_j.
\)
Since $L_r$ is nondecreasing in $r$
we have
\(
L_{i+J}=L_j\leq\ell_j.
\)
Hence
\(
L_{i+J}\leq\ell_i-m_J.
\) More generally, for $1\leq t\leq J$, the same argument gives
\(
\ell_i-m_t\geq L_{i+t}.
\)
Therefore
\[
L_{i+t}\leq\ell_i-m_t\leq U_{i+t},
\]
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:nonadj}
Let $x<y$ be consecutive elements of $\mathcal L(s)$ with
\[x\in C_i,\qquad y\in C_j,\qquad i<j.
\]
Set
\(
J=j-i,\qquad \delta=y-x.
\)
Then
\(
0<\delta\leq e.
\)

If $e\nmid d$, then
\[
\delta
=
\min
\left\{
(-dt)\bmod e:
1\leq t\leq J,\ e\nmid dt
\right\}.
\]

In particular, $\delta$ is the first positive gap above $0$ in the
finite rotation set
\[
P_J=\{(-dt)\bmod e:0\leq t\leq J\},
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\delta\in E(e,d).}
\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The inequality
\[
0<\delta\leq e
\]
follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:gapbound}.

Suppose that
\[
e\nmid d.
\]
For $1\leq t\leq J$, Lemma~\ref{lem:survival} gives
\[
x+o_t\in\mathcal L(s),
\]
where
\[
o_t=(-dt)\bmod e.
\]
Since $x$ and $y$ are consecutive and $x+o_t\geq x$, we must have
either
\(
o_t=0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
x+o_t\geq y.
\)
Equivalently,
\[
o_t=0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
o_t\geq\delta. \tag{9.5}
\]

On the other hand,
\[
\delta
=
y-x
=
-dJ+e(\ell_i-\ell_j),
\]
so
\[
\delta\equiv-dJ\pmod e.
\]
Thus
\[
o_J=\delta\bmod e. \tag{9.6}
\]

Since $e\nmid d$, the previous argument shows that
\[
\delta<e.
\]
Consequently, by (10.6),
\[
o_J=\delta>0.
\]
Combining this with (9.5), we obtain
\[
o_t=0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
o_t\geq\delta
\]
for every $1\leq t\leq J$, while $o_J=\delta$. Hence
\[
\delta
=
\min
\{o_t:1\leq t\leq J,\ o_t>0\}.
\]
Since
\[
o_t=(-dt)\bmod e,
\]
this gives
\[
\delta
=
\min
\left\{
(-dt)\bmod e:
1\leq t\leq J,\ e\nmid dt
\right\}.
\]

Thus $\delta$ is the first positive gap above $0$ in the finite rotation
set
\[
P_J=\{(-dt)\bmod e:0\leq t\leq J\}.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:euclidean-gap}, every gap in such a finite
rotation set belongs to $E(e,d)$. Therefore
\[
\delta\in E(e,d).
\]
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:nonadj-euclidean}
If $x<y$ are consecutive elements of $\mathcal L(s)$ lying in
non-adjacent columns
\[
i<j,\qquad j-i\geq2,
\]
then
\[
\boxed{y-x\in E(e,d).}
\]
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
This is an immediate consequence of Proposition~\ref{prop:nonadj}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:forward}
\[\Delta(S_h)\subseteq E(e,d) \cup \left\{M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0 \right\}.\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let
\[ \delta\in\Delta(S_h). \]
Then there exist consecutive factorization lengths
\[ \ell_1<\ell_2 \]
in some length set $\mathcal{L}(s)$ such that
\[ \delta=\ell_2-\ell_1. \]

Let $P$ and $Q$ be the corresponding lattice points in columns
$i$ and $j$, respectively.

\medskip

\noindent
\textbf{Case 1: Same column.}

If $i=j$, then the two lengths differ by exactly $e$, since
successive elements in a column differ by $e$. Therefore,
\[ \delta=e\in E(e,d). \]

\medskip

\noindent
\textbf{Case 2: Adjacent columns.}

Suppose
\[j=i+1.\]

By Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-difference-index-mapping}, if
\[P=\operatorname{Min}(i),\qquad Q=\operatorname{Max}(i+1),\]
then
\[\delta =M-re\]
for some $r\geq0$

\medskip

\noindent
\textbf{Case 3: Non-adjacent columns.}

If
\[
j-i\geq2,
\]
then 9.4. gives
\[
\delta
\in
E(e,d)
\cup
\left\{
M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0
\right\}.
\]

Therefore,
\[
\Delta(S_h)
\subseteq
E(e,d)
\cup
\left\{
M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0
\right\}.
\]
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:maintheorem}
\[
\boxed{
\Delta(S_h)
=
E(e,d)
\cup
\left\{
M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0
\right\}
}
\]
where
\[
e=h-1,
\qquad
M=
\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil(h-1)+d.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:forward} gives the forward containment
\[
\Delta(S_h)
\subseteq
E(e,d)
\cup
\left\{
M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0
\right\}.
\]

For the reverse containment, Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary-family} gives
\[\left\{M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0\right\}\subseteq
\Delta(S_h),
\]
while Proposition~\ref{corollary:Euclidean-Inclusion} gives
\[E(e,d)\subseteq\Delta(S_h).\]

Combining these two containments yields
\[\boxed{\Delta(S_h)=E(e,d)\cup\left\{M-re:r\geq0,\ M-re>0\right\}.}\]
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:basic-delta-values}
The values $d$ and $h-1$ belong to $\Delta(S_h)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
This proof proceeds trivially.
Since
\[d,h-1\in E(d,h-1),\]
and by the Euclidean containment established earlier,
\[E(d,h-1)\subseteq \Delta(S_h),\]
it follows that
\[d,h-1\in\Delta(S_h).\]
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
If $h=2$, then
\(e=h-1=1,
\)
and hence
\[
E(M,h-1)=E(M,1)=\{1,2,\ldots,M\}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:gcd-reduction}
Let
\[
g=\gcd(h-1,d),
\]
and define
\[
h'=1+\frac{h-1}{g},
\qquad
d'=\frac{d}{g}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\Delta(S_h)=g\,\Delta(S_{h'}).
}
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Set
\(
e=h-1.
\)
Then
\(
e=ge', d=gd',
\)
where
\(
e'=h'-1=\frac{h-1}{g}.
\)
Since the Euclidean algorithm is homogeneous, we have
\[
E(d,e)
=
E(gd',ge')
=
gE(d',e').
\]
Now consider the arithmetic component. Set
\[
M=\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil e+d.
\]
Using
\[
e=ge',
\qquad
d=gd',
\]
we obtain
\[
M
=
\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil ge'+gd'
=
g\left(
\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil e'+d'
\right).
\]
Define
\[
M'
=
\left\lceil\frac{a}{k}\right\rceil e'+d'.
\]
Then
\[
M=gM'.
\]
Consequently,
\[
M-re
=
gM'-rge'
=
g(M'-re').
\]
Therefore,
\[
\left\{
M-re>0 : r\geq 0
\right\}
=
g
\left\{
M'-re'>0 : r\geq 0
\right\}.
\]
By the description of the delta set,
\[
\Delta(S_h)
=
E(d,e)
\cup
\left\{
M-re>0 : r\geq 0
\right\}.
\]
\newpage
Substituting the identities above gives
\(
\Delta(S_h)
=
gE(d',e')
\cup
g
\left\{
M'-re'>0 : r\geq 0
\right\}.
\)
Factoring out \(g\), we obtain
\(
\Delta(S_h)
=
g
\left(E(d',e')\cup\left\{M'-re'>0 : r\geq 0\right\}\right).\)
Again by the description of the delta set, the expression
inside the parentheses is  \(\Delta(S_{h'}).\)
Hence\[\boxed{\Delta(S_h)=g\,\Delta(S_{h'}).}\]
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
There exist $k$ metallic Fibonacci sequences of the same order
(i.e., with the same $k$) in the delta set. Equivalently,
\[
E(P_n, P_{n-1})
=
\bigcup_{i=2}^{n}
\bigcup_{j=0}^{k-1}
\left\{ Q_i^j \right\}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
The \emph{Subtractive Euclidean Algorithm}, which we denote as $E(x,y)$, can be recursively defined in this way: 
    1. Let $x>y$. 
    2. Set $x=ky+r$. 
    Then $E(x,y) = \{x-jy: 0 \leq j \leq k-1 \} \cup E(y,r)$, with termination occurring when both terms are equal.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
$Q_i^j$ is a metallic sequence, and the delta set consists of exactly $k$ of these sequences.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Recall that a metallic fibonacci sequence is defined as $P_n = kP_{n-1} + P_{n-2}$.
    In this case, we should prove that this recurrence holds for $Q_i^{j+1}$:
    \begin{align*}
        Q_i^{j+1} &= P_{i+1} - jP_{i} \\
        &= kP_i + P_{i-1} - jP_i \\
        &= kP_{i} + P_{i-1} - j(kP_{i-1} + P_{i-2}) \\
        &= kP_i - jkP_{i-1} + P_{i-1} - jP_{i-2} \\
        &= k(P_i - jP_{i-1}) + Q_{i-1}
    \end{align*}
    \[
    Q_{i+1}^j = kQ^j + Q_{i-1}
    \]
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\[
h+1 \in C(S)
\] 
when $k > 2$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
We need $k > 2$ since this ensures that $l(n_i), l(n_j), l(n_{i+j}), l(n_0)$ can occupy different coordinates in the factorization length vector. The indices $i, j$ must satisfy
\(
i+j \leq k
\) so that enough generators can be used for $hn_0+n_{i+j}=n_i+n_j.$
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
We aim to construct an element $s \in S$ such that
\(
c(s) = h+1.
\)

Let
\[
s = hn_0 + n_{i+j},
\]
where
\[
n_0 = a, \qquad n_i = ah + id,
\]
with $i \neq j$ and
\[
i+j \leq k.
\]

Since
\[
hn_0 + n_{i+j}
=
ha + ah + (i+j)d
\]
and
\[
n_i + n_j
=
(ah + id) + (ah + jd),
\]
we obtain
\[
hn_0 + n_{i+j} = n_i + n_j.
\]

Thus, $s$ has two factorizations.

The first factorization has length
\[
|z| = h+1,
\]
while the second factorization has length
\[
|z'| = 2.
\]

Moreover,
\[
\gcd(z,z') = 0,
\]
so the two factorizations lie in distinct $R$-classes.
Therefore,
\[
c(s) = h+1,
\]
and hence
\[
h+1 \in C(S).
\]
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
if \[k \geq 3, k \leq a-2, 2\in C(s)\]
Furthermore, the set \[ [0,h+1] \] contains only \[0,2,h+1\]
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- conjecture-2: body_md -->
\[\left\lceil \frac{a-k}{k-1} \right\rceil + h+d \in C(S)\]
<!-- end conjecture-2 -->
<!-- conjecture-3: body_md -->
For \[S_h =\langle a,ah,ah+d,ah+2d,...ah+kd \rangle,\] 
\[\Delta(S_h) = E(e,d) \]
<!-- end conjecture-3 -->
